title: Designing a thread-safe class — immutable, confinement, delegation, locking strategies
shortTitle: Designing a thread-safe class — immutable, confinement, delegation, locking strategies

s1_definition.profdef: A thread-safe class can be safely used by multiple threads simultaneously without data corruption. Four strategies IN ORDER OF PREFERENCE: (1) **Immutability** — no mutable state at all. If nothing changes, nothing can be corrupted. Best strategy. (String, LocalDate, records with immutable fields). (2) **Confinement** — mutable state is NEVER shared. Each thread has its own copy: stack variables, `ThreadLocal`. No sharing = no race condition. (3) **Delegation** — delegate to existing thread-safe classes: `ConcurrentHashMap`, `AtomicInteger`, `LongAdder`, `BlockingQueue`. Let experts handle synchronization. (4) **Locking** — guard all shared mutable state with a consistent lock: `synchronized(privateFinalLock)`. Last resort — error-prone, reduces concurrency.
s1_definition.analogy: (1) **Immutable** = the bank statement is PRINTED on paper. Nobody can change it. Pass it to 100 people — zero risk. (2) **Confinement** = each teller has their OWN calculator. Nobody shares. No fights over the calculator. (3) **Delegation** = the bank buys a professional SAFE (ConcurrentHashMap) built by experts with built-in security. Don't build your own safe. (4) **Locking** = you build a custom safe with your own padlock. Works, but you might forget to lock it, or hold the key too long. Last resort.
s1_definition.oneliner: Thread safety (best to worst): Immutable (no state to corrupt) → Confinement (no sharing) → Delegation (ConcurrentHashMap/Atomic) → Locking (synchronized). Always prefer the simplest strategy.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A thread-safe class can be safely used by multiple threads simultaneously without data corruption. Four strategies IN ORDER OF PREFERENCE: (1) **Immutability** — no mutable state at all. If nothing changes, nothing can be corrupted. Best strategy. (String, LocalDate, records with immutable fields). (2) **Confinement** — mutable state is NEVER shared. Each thread has its own copy: stack variables, `ThreadLocal`. No sharing = no race condition. (3) **Delegation** — delegate to existing thread-safe classes: `ConcurrentHashMap`, `AtomicInteger`, `LongAdder`, `BlockingQueue`. Let experts handle synchronization. (4) **Locking** — guard all shared mutable state with a consistent lock: `synchronized(privateFinalLock)`. Last resort — error-prone, reduces concurrency.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** (1) **Immutable** = the bank statement is PRINTED on paper. Nobody can change it. Pass it to 100 people — zero risk. (2) **Confinement** = each teller has their OWN calculator. Nobody shares. No fights over the calculator. (3) **Delegation** = the bank buys a professional SAFE (ConcurrentHashMap) built by experts with built-in security. Don't build your own safe. (4) **Locking** = you build a custom safe with your own padlock. Works, but you might forget to lock it, or hold the key too long. Last resort.

**One line to remember:** Thread safety (best to worst): Immutable (no state to corrupt) → Confinement (no sharing) → Delegation (ConcurrentHashMap/Atomic) → Locking (synchronized). Always prefer the simplest strategy.

sections.s3_banking: **Problem — The trade service had three thread-safety bugs:** (1) `SimpleDateFormat` shared between threads (not thread-safe, garbled dates). (2) Custom cache using `HashMap` with manual synchronized — forgot to sync the `size()` check → inconsistent state. (3) Account object leaked mutable internal list of transactions via getter. Fix: (1) ThreadLocal for SimpleDateFormat (confinement). (2) Replace HashMap+synchronized with ConcurrentHashMap (delegation). (3) Return `List.copyOf(transactions)` (immutable copy).

sections.s5_journey:
**Step 1.** Immutable TradeConfirmation created. 50 threads read it simultaneously — all see the same consistent data. No locks, no synchronization, no risk.

**Step 2.** ThreadLocal gives each thread its OWN ArrayList. Thread-1's list is invisible to Thread-2. No sharing = no race condition. Cleanup with `threadLog.remove()` to prevent memory leaks.

**Step 3.** ConcurrentHashMap + AtomicInteger: 100 threads insert balances and increment counter. Zero `synchronized` blocks in our code — thread safety delegated entirely to the concurrent classes.

**Step 4.** LockedAccount: private final lock object guards balance. 100 threads debit Rs.1000 each from Rs.100,000. Final balance exactly Rs.0 — lock ensures mutual exclusion.
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  ═══ THREAD SAFETY STRATEGIES (best → worst) ═══

  1. IMMUTABLE (BEST):
     record Trade(id, amount) → all fields final → share freely!
     Zero sync. Zero risk. Zero overhead.

  2. CONFINEMENT:
     ThreadLocal<SimpleDateFormat> → each thread owns its own!
     Stack variables → never escape the method.

  3. DELEGATION:
     ConcurrentHashMap, AtomicInteger, BlockingQueue
     Zero sync in YOUR code. Experts built the thread safety.

  4. LOCKING (LAST RESORT):
     private final Object lock = new Object();
     synchronized(lock) { /* critical section */ }
     Error-prone. Keep sections SMALL. Document the policy.

  ═══ ANTI-PATTERNS ═══
  ❌ synchronized(this) → external deadlock risk
  ❌ synchronized(new Object()) → no synchronization!
  ❌ return mutableInternalList → encapsulation broken
  ❌ leak 'this' in constructor → partially-constructed object
```

sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — Thread-Safe Class Design Patterns ═══

  ┌─ IMMUTABLE (Strategy 1) ──────────────────────┐
  │  record TradeConfirmation(                     │
  │    String tradeId,        // final             │
  │    BigDecimal amount,     // immutable type     │
  │    LocalDateTime time     // immutable type     │
  │  )                                             │
  │  No sync needed. Share between any threads.    │
  └────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌─ CONFINEMENT (Strategy 2) ────────────────────┐
  │  ThreadLocal<SimpleDateFormat> formatter       │
  │  = ThreadLocal.withInitial(() -> new SDF(...))│
  │  Each thread: own instance. No sharing.        │
  │  MUST call .remove() to prevent memory leak!   │
  └────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌─ DELEGATION (Strategy 3) ─────────────────────┐
  │  class TradeCache {                            │
  │    - cache: ConcurrentHashMap<String, Trade>  │
  │    - count: AtomicLong                         │
  │    + addTrade(Trade): void  // zero sync!      │
  │    + getTrade(id): Trade    // lock-free!      │
  │  }                                             │
  │  Thread safety = delegated to CHM + Atomic.    │
  └────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌─ LOCKING (Strategy 4) ────────────────────────┐
  │  class AccountService {                        │
  │    - lock: private final Object = new Object() │
  │    - balance: BigDecimal      // guarded by lock│
  │    - lastTxnId: String        // guarded by lock│
  │    + debit(id, amt): void                      │
  │      synchronized(lock) { check + update }     │
  │  }                                             │
  │  Rules: private lock, final lock, small section│
  └────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ═══ SOLID ═══
  S: Each strategy class has one responsibility
  O: Add new strategies without changing existing
  D: Depend on ConcurrentMap interface, not HashMap impl
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Designing a thread-safe class follows four strategies in preference order. First, IMMUTABILITY — if nothing changes, nothing can corrupt. Records with immutable fields (String, BigDecimal, LocalDateTime) are freely shareable with zero synchronization. Second, CONFINEMENT — mutable state that is never shared. Stack-local variables and ThreadLocal give each thread its own copy. Third, DELEGATION — use existing thread-safe classes (ConcurrentHashMap, AtomicInteger, BlockingQueue) instead of writing your own synchronization. Zero `synchronized` in your code — experts handle thread safety. Fourth and last resort, LOCKING — `synchronized(privateFinalLock)` guards shared mutable state. Keep critical sections small, use a private final lock object (never `this`), and document which lock guards which state.

Anti-patterns to avoid: `synchronized(this)` exposes the lock externally (deadlock risk). `synchronized(new Object())` creates a new lock every time (no synchronization!). Leaking mutable internal state via getters (return `List.copyOf()` instead). Publishing `this` during construction (another thread sees a half-built object). In banking: trade confirmation is an immutable record (strategy 1). Date formatting uses ThreadLocal (strategy 2). Trade cache uses ConcurrentHashMap (strategy 3). Balance update uses private final lock (strategy 4 — only for complex multi-field updates).
